name: Stellar
executive_summary: Stellar has run for eleven years as a payments network and, since 2024, has carried a modern Rust/WASM smart contract layer alongside it. The published TradFi score would improve if a dedicated spot trading vehicle existed; that single missing piece is what holds it to 65 against fundamentals that earn 69.56. The institutions that would use such a vehicle are already building here, with Franklin Templeton running a validator and using Stellar as primary tokenization infrastructure and DTCC targeting H1 2027 for DTC-custodied assets. On the agent axis the score is uncapped and lands at 65 on its own merits, with near-zero fees, no public mempool and protocol-native delegation on one side, and five-second settlement, no confidentiality in production and an agent toolset with no visible users on the other.

binding_cap.short_note: Capped by Regulatory Clarity Partial -- named in the March 2026 SEC-CFTC digital commodities release and CME futures are live, but no dedicated spot vehicle exists.

key_findings: Stellar landed in the middle ground -- 'Partial,' not a full pass -- on all three of our baseline checks: quantum-computer readiness, regulatory footing, and security track record. Of the three, only the regulatory check actually holds the score down: based purely on its category-by-category performance, Stellar would score about 70, but its still-partial regulatory standing (no dedicated spot trading vehicle exists yet) cuts that to the published 65.

Regulatory & Risk is a strength at 84. Stellar has never been sued or investigated by regulators, has received two favorable early guidance letters from the SEC confirming it wouldn't take enforcement action on specific matters, and is stewarded by a US non-profit that publishes its own financial records publicly.

Real-World Utility scores 82, covering two genuinely live businesses: Stellar processed a record $5.5 billion in payment volume in the first quarter of 2026, and the value of real-world assets tokenized on the network roughly doubled quarter over quarter to about $3 billion. The score is held back by concentration, though -- roughly 19,000 holders across about 70 tokenized assets looks more like accredited, professional distribution than broad retail reach.

Tokenomics & Supply scores 66. On the positive side: a hard supply cap, zero inflation since 2019, and transparent, categorized accounting of where the supply sits. Weighing against it: the foundation controls a treasury of roughly 15.17 billion XLM with no published schedule for when or how it might be released, and holders capture almost no direct value from network activity -- transaction fees are permanently removed from circulation rather than paid out to validators or token holders.

Decentralization is held down by a real trade-off, and the trade-off cuts against holders. A small group of validators can freeze funds, and has done so twice: containing the network's own corrupted data in October 2025, and freezing roughly 48 million XLM belonging to an attacker in February 2026. Both actions were publicly disclosed and aimed at stopping harm, which is the good version of this capability. It is still a capability, though, now written into the protocol itself, and a ledger where roughly ten organizations can vote to freeze an account is meaningfully less permissionless than one where nobody can.

Privacy & Confidentiality scores 38. Stellar has built basic zero-knowledge cryptography tools directly into its smart contract platform, giving developers real building blocks for privacy features. A more complete feature that would let token amounts be hidden (Confidential Tokens) is still in early testing with its security audits incomplete, so it earns no credit here yet.

Operational Reliability passes on a record with no mainnet halt in over seven years. Contemporaneous reporting of a ten-hour outage in April 2021 describes an event that did not happen to the network -- SDF's own validators and public API went down while the rest of the network kept closing ledgers.

Settlement speed is the clearest structural concern for agent use. A Stellar transaction becomes irreversible once the ledger closes, which takes about five to six seconds in practice. That finality is genuine -- no waiting on confirmations, no risk of the transaction being undone later -- but five seconds is slow for software that needs to act, check the result and act again. The network cannot currently be configured to close faster than four seconds, so this is not something a settings change fixes. It did not cap the score, and it is still the hardest limit on how agents can use this chain today.

Economic Predictability is Stellar's strongest category at 78. There's no public staging area where pending transactions can be seen and front-run, tied fees are broken randomly rather than by who pays more, and during a fee surge everyone pays the same clearing price rather than bidding against each other. Validators also earn no fees, no staking rewards, and can't profit by reordering transactions. The score is held down by the same freezing capability noted above: a validator group can freeze accounts, and has.

Composability & Atomicity (72) is a split result. Stellar's original payment layer is excellent at this: up to 100 steps can be bundled into a single transaction that either fully succeeds or fully fails, with nothing left half-done and no helper contract needed. The newer smart contract layer does not join up with it the same way -- a contract call cannot be bundled with those payment steps in one transaction. Developers work around it by routing everything through a contract, which works and is the standard pattern here, but it is extra work that some networks do not ask for.

Agent Tooling (63) is capability without evidence of demand. Stellar has built a genuinely complete set of tools for AI agents: a server that lets an agent query the network directly, an official library of agent instructions covering most of the stack, and two separate standards for machine-to-machine payments. Building that before the demand arrives is a defensible bet. What is missing is anyone visibly using it -- no published usage figures, no named projects running in production, and no record of agent payments actually settling here. Scored as readiness rather than adoption, and it will move up quickly if real traffic appears.

Agent Identity & Compliance scores 58, splitting into a real strength and a real gap. The strength: Stellar has genuine tools for controlling what an agent can do, including signers that can enforce spending limits, address allow-lists, and time windows, plus newer protocol features (CAP-71 and CAP-72) purpose-built for this kind of delegation. The gap: there's no registry for identifying which agent is which, no standard way to formally link an agent back to the human or organization that controls it, and no system for issuing verifiable credentials to agents.

watch_items: A live, dedicated spot trading vehicle (like a spot ETF) for XLM is the single highest-impact pending event for this chain -- it would move the regulatory check from a partial pass to a full one and add the 4.56 points currently being held back. Grayscale has filed the paperwork (an S-1 registration) seeking an exchange listing for a Stellar trust, the closest thing currently in progress. A futures-based ETF and a small roughly 3% position inside a broader multi-asset ETF already exist but don't count as the kind of dedicated, direct access this check requires.

Confidential Tokens, the feature that would let token amounts be hidden, has been in early testing since late June 2026, with security audits underway but not yet complete. If and when it reaches mainnet, it would raise the Privacy & Confidentiality score on both frameworks.

An early-stage proposal (CAP-0087) for quantum-resistant transaction signing exists in draft form with no confirmed timeline for shipping. If activated, it would add quantum protection to Stellar's authentication -- but only for accounts that opt in to the newer smart-contract account type, leaving older-style accounts still using quantum-vulnerable cryptography.

A network upgrade (Protocol 28) goes to a validator vote on September 16, 2026, bundling several technical improvements aimed at making the time between ledger closes more consistent by requiring validators to keep their clocks precisely synchronized. It would make settlement timing more predictable but would not bring it under one second.

The number of top-tier validator organizations securing the network was announced as expanding from seven to ten on July 16, 2026, with full integration into the network's trust structure expected by mid-August but not yet confirmed complete. Re-check the current validator count before citing it.

Every validator on Stellar currently runs the same underlying software (stellar-core), and a February 2026 incident showed the same single-point-of-failure pattern on the data-query side too -- one shared software bug took down multiple independent data providers at once, since they all ran the same code. If a genuinely independent second implementation of either piece of software is built and adopted, that would be grounds to raise the relevant scores.

The most recent published independent security audit of Stellar's core software covers an older version (v25.0.0), while the network currently runs a newer one (v27). A published audit of the current version would close this gap in the security track record.
